element_a.enriched_content: The formula computes the generalized false-positive rate for a perfectly calibrated classifier within group G_t. It takes the difference between the group-average prediction E[h_t(x)] and the group-average squared prediction E[h_t(x)^2], which captures how much probability mass the classifier assigns without being overly concentrated near 0 or 1. element_a.enriched_content: The inequality upper-bounds the true expected Wasserstein-1 mismatch between each group’s score distribution and a common reference (the barycenter) by the same mismatch computed from empirical (sampled) distributions, plus a slack term \epsilon. variables.Enc: encoder mapping x to latent factors (e1, e2)

variables.Dis1: discriminator predicting e2 from e1 (to enforce independence)
variables.Dis2: discriminator predicting e1 from e2 (to enforce independence)

element_a.enriched_content: The equation defines a joint min–max training objective where the encoder, predictor, and decoder are optimized to minimize a total cost J, while two discriminators are optimized to maximize their ability to infer one latent from the other. The total cost combines (i) a supervised prediction loss that makes e1 informative for predicting y, (ii) a reconstruction/decoding loss that forces the pair (psi(e1), e2) to retain enough information to reproduce x, and (iii) an adversarial disentanglement term that penalizes mutual predictability between e1 and e2 by training Dis1 and Dis2 against the encoder. In the paper’s method, this encourages e1 to become invariant to nuisance factors (e.g., lighting) while e2 captures the remaining variation, yielding improved invariance metrics.
